area.summary: Land Area (km²) measures a country’s total surface, indicating spatial capacity for agriculture, settlements, and resources. Largest: Russia, Canada, China, United States, Brazil, Australia. Smallest: Vatican City, Monaco, Nauru, Tuvalu, San Marino, Liechtenstein. Regional patterns: Africa has several very large states (Algeria, DRC, Sudan); Europe is fragmented with many small/medium countries and microstates; Oceania is polarized (Australia vs numerous tiny islands); Asia spans mega-territories and compacts (Kazakhstan/China vs Singapore/Maldives). Land area is mostly stable; marginal changes come from reclamation, erosion, or sea-level rise affecting low-lying islands. Correlations (Society & Governance): Larger area often links to lower density, higher service delivery and infrastructure reach costs, more decentralization and resource dependence; small areas to higher urbanization and tighter administrative coverage. Outlook: Rankings steady; climate and coastal dynamics will shape edge cases.

population.summary: Population measures how many people live in a country at a point in time, shaping demand for services, labor supply, and policy. Largest populations: India, China, United States, Indonesia, Pakistan; smallest: Vatican City, Tuvalu, Nauru, San Marino, Monaco. Trends: fastest growth in Sub‑Saharan Africa (e.g., Nigeria, Ethiopia, DRC) and parts of the Middle East; slowing or negative growth in East Asia (China, Japan, Korea) and much of Europe; South Asia is moderating. Regional patterns reflect fertility, mortality, and migration; small high‑income states often rely on net immigration. Correlations within Society & Governance: higher population and density raise service delivery needs and urbanization; age structure shapes dependency ratios and demographic distribution; migration influences social cohesion and labor force size. Outlook: global growth is decelerating, likely peaking mid‑to‑late century, with population weight shifting toward Africa.

population_growth.summary: Population Growth (% per year) tracks annual population change from births, deaths, and net migration. Highest rates persist in Sub‑Saharan Africa (e.g., Niger, DRC), and in some Gulf states via migration; the lowest or negative growth appears in East Asia and Europe (e.g., Japan, China, Bulgaria, Italy). Regional patterns: Africa remains youthful and expanding; South Asia and Latin America are slowing; Europe and East Asia are aging and shrinking. Correlations in Society & Governance: positive with fertility and youth dependency; negative with life expectancy, female education, and urbanization; governance and economic opportunity attract migrants, lifting growth. Outlook: global growth keeps decelerating, more countries enter zero/negative territory, while Africa drives most net additions; migration will be the main stabilizer.

median_age.summary: Median Age (years) is the age at which half the population is younger and half older—an anchor for understanding workforce supply, healthcare demand, and dependency. Highest values are found in Japan (~49) and much of Southern/Western Europe (Italy, Germany, Spain, Portugal), reflecting low fertility and long life expectancy. Lowest are in Sub‑Saharan Africa—Niger (~15), Uganda, Mali, Somalia—driven by high birth rates and improving but still lower longevity. Regions: Europe and East Asia are aging fast; Eastern Europe adds out‑migration; Latin America sits in the mid‑30s and rising; MENA is trending older; Gulf states are skewed by migrant-heavy working ages. Correlations in Society & Governance: higher median age typically links to lower population growth, higher old‑age dependency, lower youth dependency, higher life expectancy, and different migration patterns. Outlook: continued global aging, with pension/healthcare pressures in older societies and a youth bulge opportunity in Africa if jobs and education keep pace.

fertility_rate.summary: Fertility Rate (births per woman) gauges the average number of children per woman—shaping population growth, age structure, and planning. Highest levels persist in Sub‑Saharan Africa (e.g., Niger, DR Congo, Somalia); the lowest are in high‑income East Asia and Europe (e.g., South Korea, Singapore, Italy, Spain), often well below the ~2.1 replacement level. Regional pattern: SSA high but gradually falling; South Asia and MENA mid and declining; Latin America near/below replacement; Europe/East Asia persistently very low. Correlates positively with population growth and child dependency, and inversely with female education, urbanization, income, and access to reproductive health; higher fertility often aligns with weaker maternal health outcomes. Trend: global decline and later births. Outlook: ongoing declines where education and urbanization rise; only modest policy‑driven rebounds; aging and labor‑force pressures will grow.

urbanization_rate.summary: Urbanization Rate (%) is the share of a country’s population living in urban areas. Leaders are near‑100% city‑states and Gulf economies (Singapore, Hong Kong, Qatar, Kuwait, UAE) and much of Latin America and Western Europe (80–90%+). Laggards remain agrarian Sub‑Saharan Africa and parts of South Asia (e.g., Burundi, Niger, Ethiopia, Nepal) often below 30%. Trend: rising almost everywhere; Latin America/Europe are high and stable, while Africa and South/Southeast Asia see the fastest gains and growth of secondary cities. Correlates positively with GDP per capita, access to services (water, sanitation, health, education), internet use, and government effectiveness; but also with housing pressure, congestion, inequality, and informality. Often links to lower fertility and slower population growth. Outlook: continued climb, especially in Africa; policy focus on planned, inclusive, resilient urban growth.

democracy_index.summary: The Democracy Index (0–10) gauges the quality of electoral processes, political participation, government functioning, and civil liberties. Top performers include Norway, Iceland, Sweden, Finland, Denmark, and New Zealand; lowest scores cluster in North Korea, Afghanistan, Syria, Eritrea, and Myanmar. Regional patterns: Western Europe leads; North America is high but with concerns (e.g., polarization in the US); Latin America is uneven; Asia-Pacific spans high (NZ, Australia) to authoritarian (China, Vietnam); MENA and the Sahel are lowest amid conflict and coups; Eastern Europe/Central Asia are mixed with deep backsliding in Russia. Trend: a gradual global decline since the mid-2010s, punctuated by occasional reforms. Strong correlations with Freedom Index, Rule of Law, lower corruption, and Political Stability (though transitions can be volatile). Outlook: a dense election cycle and conflicts keep risks elevated; media freedom, judicial independence, and inclusive institutions are pivotal for recovery.

press_freedom_index.summary: Press Freedom Index (index) measures journalists’ ability to report without censorship or retaliation, shaped by laws, state/market pressures, violence, and media pluralism. Top performers: Nordic countries (Norway, Finland, Sweden, Denmark) and the Netherlands. Low performers: North Korea, Eritrea, Turkmenistan, Syria, Iran. Regional patterns: Europe leads; the Americas are mixed; Sub‑Saharan Africa is heterogeneous; MENA and parts of Asia/CIS score low, especially in conflict zones. Trends: gradual erosion in several democracies (polarization, SLAPPs, media capture), severe repression in autocracies; targeted legal reforms and safety initiatives yield pockets of improvement. Correlations: strongly aligned with civil liberties, political rights, rule of law, and low corruption; inversely with conflict and internet shutdowns. Outlook: Risks from wars, digital harassment, and AI disinformation; progress hinges on legal safeguards, independent regulators, and journalist safety.

world_happiness_index.summary: The World Happiness Index (0–10) captures self-reported life satisfaction, influenced by income, social support, freedom, and perceived corruption. Top performers remain the Nordics—Finland, Denmark, Iceland, Sweden—plus Switzerland and the Netherlands; lowest scores persist in conflict-affected or fragile states such as Afghanistan and Lebanon, and parts of Sub-Saharan Africa. Regional patterns: Western Europe and Oceania are high; Latin America is mid-high buoyed by social ties; East Asia is mixed; MENA and South Asia vary widely. Trends show stable Nordic leadership, some youth declines in richer countries, and uneven post-pandemic recovery. Strong positive links with Society & Governance peers: social equality, low corruption/trust in institutions, personal safety, civic participation, and better mental health; income alone is insufficient without inclusion and rights. Outlook: gradual gains where governance and social protection strengthen; conflicts, inflation, and climate stress are headwinds.

gdp.summary:
GDP (current US$) measures the total market value of goods and services produced in nominal US dollars (Unit: USD). It reflects economic size and near-term health; driven by consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports, and is sensitive to inflation and exchange rates.

Top: United States by a wide margin, then China; Japan, Germany, and India follow. Low: microstates (e.g., Tuvalu, Nauru) and fragile economies (e.g., South Sudan) record the smallest totals.

Trends: Rapid gains in emerging Asia; resilient US; slower Europe; oil exporters volatile with energy prices; Sub‑Saharan Africa expanding from a low base.

Correlations (Economy & Labor): Higher GDP aligns with lower unemployment, higher wages, labor productivity, export revenues, and FDI; nominal increases can reflect price changes as much as real output.

Outlook: Moderately positive but uneven; tech/AI and the green transition support growth, while rates, debt, and geopolitics pose risks.

gdp_per_capita_current_us.summary: GDP per Capita (current US$) gauges average economic output per person (GDP/population) and is a proxy for living standards in USD. Top performers include Luxembourg, Ireland, Switzerland, Singapore, Qatar, Norway, and the United States; lowest levels are seen in Burundi, South Sudan, Central African Republic, Malawi, Niger, and DRC. Trends: long-run global rise, a pandemic dip in 2020 with rebound; volatility in commodity-dependent and tourism economies; very high figures in small financial hubs reflect MNE accounting. Regional gaps persist—OECD/high‑income far above Sub‑Saharan Africa; East Asia continues convergence; Latin America often stagnates. Correlates strongly with labor productivity, formal employment, wages, investment, and trade openness; inversely with unemployment/informality. Note that inequality and exchange rates can distort interpretation in current dollars. Outlook: moderate but uneven gains, with AI, energy and geopolitical shifts likely to widen divergence.

gni_per_capita_current_us.summary: GNI per capita (current US$) measures average resident income, including cross‑border earnings, expressed in USD—useful for comparing living standards but sensitive to exchange rates and population size. Top performers are high‑income economies and financial/resource hubs (Luxembourg, Switzerland, Norway, Singapore, Qatar, United States), while lowest values cluster in fragile Sub‑Saharan states (Burundi, South Sudan, Malawi, Central African Republic, DRC). Regional gaps persist: North America, Western Europe, and advanced Asia far exceed South Asia and Sub‑Saharan Africa; Gulf states outpace MENA peers. It closely tracks GDP per capita and correlates with higher labor productivity, formal wages, and lower poverty/unemployment, though inequality can mask distribution. Commodity cycles and remittances can shift GNI independently of domestic output. Outlook: gradual gains in emerging Asia; divergence elsewhere as FX and commodities drive near‑term moves.

gini_index.summary: The Gini Index (0–100) gauges income inequality; lower values mean a more equal income distribution. Top performers include Slovenia, Czechia, Slovakia and the Nordics (mid‑20s). Low performers are led by South Africa and Namibia (60+), with Brazil and Colombia also high (50s). Regional pattern: Europe is most equal; Southern Africa and much of Latin America are most unequal; East Asia is moderate (Japan/Korea low‑30s; China high‑30s/low‑40s); the US sits in the low‑40s. Recent trend: mild post‑pandemic rises where inflation outpaced wage gains; robust transfers in Europe tempered increases. Correlations in Economy & Labor: higher Gini often coexists with higher poverty rates, greater informality, and weaker wage growth at the bottom; strong redistribution and collective bargaining align with lower Gini. Outlook: If real wages recover and social supports persist, inequality may edge down, but commodity and housing cost pressures are risks.

public_debt_of_gdp.summary: Public Debt (% of GDP) tracks central government gross debt relative to economic output, signaling fiscal space and repayment capacity (lower is generally better). Top performers with low debt include Estonia, Luxembourg, Norway, Hong Kong, and Botswana; highest ratios are seen in Japan, Greece, Italy, Lebanon, and Sudan. Trends: Debt jumped after 2008 and COVID-19; advanced economies remain elevated, while some commodity exporters and Baltics stay comparatively low. Several emerging markets face rising burdens from weak growth, currency depreciation, and tighter global financing. Correlations within Economy & Labor: higher debt typically accompanies persistent budget deficits, larger interest outlays, and slower growth; consolidation phases can weigh on employment and public investment. Outlook: With higher rates and aging pressures, fiscal consolidation will stay on agendas; stabilizing or reducing ratios hinges on sustained growth, disciplined budgets, and efficient debt management.

tax_revenue_of_gdp.summary: Tax Revenue (% of GDP) shows how much of a country’s output is collected in taxes to fund public services. Top shares are in Nordic and Western Europe (e.g., Denmark, France, Belgium, Finland) with broad bases and strong compliance. Lowest ratios are common in low‑income Sub‑Saharan Africa and some resource‑rich economies with low taxes (e.g., Nigeria, DRC, Gulf states) and parts of South Asia/Central America, often single to low‑teens. Regional pattern: OECD high/stable; Latin America mid and rising; East Asia mixed; Sub‑Saharan Africa lower with gradual gains. Pandemic caused a 2020 dip, then rebound with recovery and commodity prices. Correlates positively with GDP per capita and labor productivity, negatively with informality; higher ratios align with lower deficits and steadier public investment; cyclical ties to unemployment/inflation. Outlook: modest gains via base‑broadening and digital compliance, tempered by informality, slow growth, and tax competition.

unemployment_rate.summary: Unemployment Rate (%): Share of the labor force seeking work but jobless. Lower values indicate tighter labor markets. Top performers typically include Switzerland, Japan, Czechia, and Singapore (low single digits), reflecting strong demand and aging demographics. High rates persist in South Africa (very high), and remain elevated—though improving—in parts of Southern Europe (e.g., Spain, Greece) and North Africa/West Asia, with youth unemployment especially acute. Trends: Post‑pandemic recovery drove lows in many advanced economies; 2024 showed mild upticks in Europe as growth cooled, while the U.S. stayed tight. Correlations (Economy & Labor): inversely with GDP growth and job creation (Okun’s law); linked to participation, vacancies, wage growth, and under/employment mix—low participation can mask slack. Outlook: Slight softening if growth slows, but advanced economies likely remain relatively low; structural reforms and re‑skilling are key where unemployment is entrenched.

big_mac_index.summary: Big Mac Index (unit: index) gauges local purchasing power and currency misvaluation by comparing Big Mac prices across countries. Highest readings are typically in high‑income Europe (e.g., Switzerland, Norway, Denmark), while lowest are common in emerging markets (e.g., Egypt, India, Turkey), reflecting weaker currencies and lower wage/ingredient costs. Regional patterns: rich Europe/North America are pricier; South Asia, North Africa and parts of Sub‑Saharan Africa are cheaper; Japan often appears undervalued amid yen weakness; Latin America shows volatility with inflation. The index correlates positively with GDP per capita, wages and cost‑of‑living, and moves with inflation and exchange rates in the Economy & Labor cluster; input costs (beef, wheat) matter too. Outlook: with disinflation in advanced economies but uneven FX, expect slower price gains yet continued rank reshuffles driven by currency moves and wage/food costs.

human_development_index_hdi.summary: HDI (0–1) summarizes human development via life expectancy (health), education, and income (standard of living). Top performers consistently include Switzerland, Norway, Iceland, Hong Kong, and Singapore; lowest scores are found in Niger, South Sudan, Central African Republic, and Chad. Regional gaps persist: OECD and parts of East Asia/Pacific are very high; Latin America and Eastern Europe are high but uneven; South Asia and MENA are mid-range; Sub‑Saharan Africa lags, especially in fragile states. After COVID‑19 declines, many countries rebounded, but recovery is incomplete and unequal. HDI correlates strongly with life expectancy, infant/maternal mortality (inverse), school attainment/literacy, poverty (inverse), and health spending per capita, reflecting broader social capacity. Outlook: moderate global gains with investments in health, education, and inclusive growth, tempered by conflict, climate stress, and inequality.

health_expenditure_per_capita.summary: Health Expenditure per Capita (USD) measures average annual health spending per person, indicating capacity to fund services and quality of care. Highest levels are in the US and wealthy Europe (e.g., Switzerland, Norway/Luxembourg); lowest in low‑income Sub‑Saharan Africa (e.g., Burundi, DRC, Niger) and parts of South Asia (e.g., Bangladesh). Regional pattern: North America/Western Europe very high; OECD rising; Central/Eastern Europe converging; East Asia and GCC growing fast; Latin America mid; SSA lowest. Typically correlates positively with life expectancy, immunization, physician density, and UHC coverage, and negatively with infant/under‑5 mortality—though efficiency and price differences create outliers. Outlook: continued upward pressure from aging and chronic disease, with fiscal constraints driving shifts toward value, primary care, and prevention.

physicians_per_1_000_people.summary: Physicians per 1,000 measures doctor availability and thus access to care. Top densities appear in Cuba (~8), Greece and Austria (~5–6), Germany and Norway (~4–5). Lowest levels are in parts of Sub‑Saharan Africa—Niger, Chad, Somalia, Ethiopia—often ≤0.1–0.3; South Asia (Afghanistan, Bangladesh) remains <1, while India is ~1–1.2. Europe and some high‑income Gulf states cluster high; Latin America and East Asia are mixed; large rural‑urban gaps persist. The metric correlates positively with hospital beds per 1,000 and health expenditure, and inversely with maternal/infant mortality; outcomes also hinge on physician distribution and the skill mix (nurses, primary care). Trend: slow global gains, but aging populations, burnout, and emigration strain supply. Outlook: modest improvement via expanded training, international recruitment, task‑shifting, and telehealth, with equitable distribution the main challenge.

hospital_beds_per_1_000_people.summary: Hospital Beds per 1,000 People gauges inpatient capacity and surge readiness. Top densities are seen in Japan, South Korea, Germany, Austria, and parts of Central/Eastern Europe; lowest levels prevail in many Sub‑Saharan African and South Asian countries (e.g., Nigeria, Ethiopia, Bangladesh) and parts of Central America. Regional pattern: East Asia and continental Europe are high; Anglo countries (US, UK, Canada) are relatively low for advanced economies; MENA/Latin America sit mid‑range. Long‑run OECD trend is declining beds due to day surgery and shorter stays, while China and some Eastern Europe maintained or expanded supply; COVID‑19 spurred selective ICU/surge additions. The metric correlates positively with health spending, physician/nurse density, hospital admissions, length of stay, and aging (old‑age dependency), but does not guarantee better outcomes without staffing and quality. Outlook: gradual right‑sizing, more flexible/ICU capacity, and workforce/primary care investment to balance resilience and efficiency.

infant_mortality_rate.summary: Measures infant deaths per 1,000 live births—an acute proxy for health system performance, maternal health, nutrition, and social conditions. Top performers (lowest rates): Iceland, Japan, Singapore, Finland, Norway. Low performers (highest rates): Somalia, Nigeria, Chad, Central African Republic, Sierra Leone (often 50+). Regional pattern: Europe and East Asia are lowest; Sub‑Saharan Africa and parts of South Asia are highest; the U.S. underperforms OECD peers due to prematurity and inequities. Trend: global declines continue, but gains lag in fragile, rural, and conflict‑affected settings; neonatal deaths now form a larger share. Strong correlations with maternal mortality, under‑5 mortality, immunization and skilled birth attendance, WASH access, poverty/education, and health spending. Outlook: further declines are likely with scaled newborn care, vaccines, nutrition, and clean water/sanitation—if coverage gaps and inequalities are reduced.

maternal_mortality_ratio.summary:
Maternal Mortality Ratio (per 100,000 live births) measures deaths from pregnancy-related causes, reflecting quality and access of maternal care.

Top performers: Norway, Finland, Iceland, Italy, Spain, Japan (often single-digit to low-teen rates). Lowest performers: South Sudan, Chad, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Somalia, Afghanistan (frequently >400).

Trends/regional: Strong declines since 2000 in South Asia (e.g., India) and parts of East Africa; progress has stalled in many places since ~2016 with pandemic setbacks. Sub‑Saharan Africa bears most deaths; Latin America/Caribbean has plateaued; the United States remains higher than peer OECD countries.

Correlations (Health & Social): closely tied to neonatal mortality, skilled birth attendance and antenatal care coverage, adolescent fertility, health worker density, health spending, women’s education, and poverty.

Outlook: Further reductions depend on midwife-led care, emergency obstetrics, reliable referral/transport, respectful care, and family planning, supported by stronger data and post-pandemic recovery.

life_expectancy_at_birth.summary: Life Expectancy at Birth (years) measures the average years a newborn is expected to live if current mortality rates persist—an integrative proxy for population health. Leaders include Hong Kong SAR, Japan, Singapore, Switzerland, and Spain; lowest values are concentrated in Sub‑Saharan Africa (e.g., Lesotho, Central African Rep., Chad, Sierra Leone, Nigeria). Regional patterns: Western Europe and East Asia are highest; North America is mixed with the U.S. lagging peers; Latin America saw notable COVID‑era setbacks; conflict‑affected states remain depressed. Strong correlations: negative with infant/maternal mortality, HIV/TB and air pollution; positive with UHC coverage, immunization, health spending, sanitation, and education. Trend: decades of gains, a COVID dip and partial rebound, with plateauing in some high‑income settings due to NCDs and overdoses. Outlook: gradual recovery, hinging on primary care, NCD prevention, and environmental health; risks from conflict and climate.

adult_literacy_rate.summary: Adult Literacy Rate (% of people 15+) gauges basic reading/writing skills, a foundation for empowerment and growth. Top performers: most OECD, Eastern Europe, and East Asia at 97–100% (e.g., Japan, Poland, Finland). Lowest rates persist in parts of Sub‑Saharan Africa and conflict‑affected states (e.g., Niger, South Sudan, Chad, Afghanistan), often below 50–60%. Regional patterns: Latin America and MENA are mostly high but with gender gaps in some countries; South Asia improving; SSA shows slow gains, with large rural–urban and gender disparities. Correlations within Health & Social: higher literacy aligns with longer life expectancy, lower child/maternal mortality, better vaccination uptake, lower fertility, and higher incomes. Trend: global literacy is rising, with youth outpacing adults. Outlook: continued gains likely via universal schooling and targeted female/adult learning, though conflict and funding gaps remain key risks.

homelessness_rate.summary:
Measures people without a permanent home per 10,000 inhabitants, signaling housing exclusion and social stress. Top performers (lowest rates): Finland and other Nordics using Housing First with robust safety nets; Singapore/Japan also report low rates. Low performers (highest rates): New Zealand, Australia, and the United States, where high housing costs and limited social housing lift prevalence (note differing definitions).

Trends/regional: Rising in many high‑cost, urbanized regions; flat or declining where prevention, rapid rehousing, and social housing expanded (e.g., Finland, Denmark). Big-city rates exceed rural.

Correlations within Health & Social: positive with poverty risk, unemployment, housing cost overburden, mental ill‑health and substance use; negative with social protection spending, affordable housing stock, and access to community care.

Outlook: Without faster housing supply and income supports, rates likely stay elevated; scaling Housing First plus prevention can bend the curve.

old_age_dependency_ratio.summary: The Old-Age Dependency Ratio (% 65+ relative to ages 15–64) gauges potential support pressure on workers and public finances; higher values imply more retirees per worker. Highest ratios are seen in Japan and much of Europe (Italy, Germany, Spain, Portugal, Finland), with South Korea accelerating. Lowest are in Sub‑Saharan Africa (e.g., Niger, Uganda) and parts of the Middle East/South Asia (e.g., Qatar, UAE, Pakistan), reflecting high fertility and/or young migrant workforces. Regional patterns: Europe and East Asia are oldest; Latin America is mid but rising; Africa remains low but will climb. Correlates within Society & Governance include higher life expectancy and median age (+), lower fertility (−), and increased healthcare and pension outlays (+); higher older‑age labor participation and immigration can mitigate strain. Outlook: Ratios will rise broadly; reforms around retirement age, workforce inclusion, managed migration, and preventive health are key to sustainability.

age_dependency_ratio_total.summary: Age Dependency Ratio (Total) measures dependents (0–14 and 65+) relative to working-age (15–64); higher values imply greater fiscal and social support pressure per worker. Lowest ratios (strongest support base) are typically in Gulf states with large migrant workforces (UAE, Qatar, Kuwait). Highest ratios are concentrated in Sub‑Saharan Africa due to high fertility (Niger, DR Congo, Uganda, Mali). Outside Africa, aging drives high ratios in Japan and parts of Southern Europe (Italy, Greece). Regional trends: falling child dependency in many African and South Asian countries, but still elevated; rising old‑age dependency in Europe and East Asia; Latin America near the bottom of its demographic dividend. Correlates with fertility, median age, labor force participation, social protection and health/pension spending. Outlook: global ratios will edge up as populations age; boosting female/youth employment, smart migration, and pension/retirement reforms can mitigate pressures.

overall_immunization_coverage.summary:
Overall Immunization Coverage (%) measures the share of children completing core vaccines (measles, polio, DTP), indicating system reach, supply chains, and public trust.

Top performers: most high‑income Europe/East Asia and several LMIC standouts (e.g., Rwanda, Bangladesh, Vietnam, Cuba) often exceed 90–95%. Low performers cluster in fragile/conflict states and remote areas of Sub‑Saharan Africa and parts of South Asia (e.g., Somalia, South Sudan, Afghanistan, Yemen), with large urban–rural and wealth gaps.

Trends: long‑run gains have stalled in some places; COVID‑19 disruptions caused backsliding. Latin America remains high; South Asia improved but uneven; Sub‑Saharan Africa is mixed with pockets of progress.

Correlates: lower under‑5 mortality, higher skilled birth attendance, health spend, female education, and WASH; negatively with poverty, conflict, and hesitancy.

Outlook: gradual recovery via catch‑up drives and Gavi support; equity and trust efforts are key to restoring >90%.

extreme_poverty.summary: Extreme Poverty (% of population) measures the share living on less than $2.15/day (PPP), capturing severe deprivation in basic needs. Top performers with near‑zero rates include most high‑income economies (Nordics, Western Europe, Japan, Korea, Singapore, Canada, U.S.). Lowest performers are concentrated in Sub‑Saharan Africa (e.g., South Sudan, Burundi, Central African Republic, Madagascar, DR Congo, Mozambique, Niger), with fragile/conflict states like Afghanistan and Yemen also elevated. Trend: sharp global declines since 2000 slowed and briefly reversed during COVID‑19; recovery is uneven, with SSA now hosting most of the world’s extreme poor, while South and parts of Southeast Asia saw large reductions. Strong correlations appear with low education access, weak healthcare coverage, high child/maternal mortality, undernutrition, and limited social protection. Outlook: gradual improvement if growth and disinflation hold; risks from conflict, climate shocks, and food prices persist. Targeted cash transfers and education/health investments are pivotal.

access_to_basic_drinking_water.summary: Access to Basic Drinking Water measures the share (%) of people with reliable access to safe, clean drinking water. Top performers (≈99–100%) are high-income countries such as Singapore, Iceland, Switzerland, Japan, and the Netherlands. Lowest access persists in fragile/arid states including South Sudan, Somalia, Chad, Haiti, and Papua New Guinea. Regional patterns: Europe/North America, East Asia, and the GCC are near universal; Sub‑Saharan Africa (Sahel, Horn) and parts of South Asia lag, with pronounced rural–urban gaps. Trend: steady global gains, especially in South and Southeast Asia, but climate stress, groundwater depletion, and conflict slow progress. Correlates strongly with sanitation access, lower under‑5 mortality and diarrheal disease, and higher life expectancy and school attendance. Outlook: gradual improvement with sustained investment and climate‑resilient systems; fragile contexts remain at risk without governance and humanitarian support.

co2_emissions.summary: CO₂ Emissions measures total tonnes of CO₂ a country releases yearly, driven by energy mix, industry, transport, and population. Lower is better. Highest emitters (absolute): China, United States, India, Russia, and the EU bloc; lowest: small island states (e.g., Tuvalu, Kiribati), Bhutan, and several least‑developed African economies. Trends: long‑term declines in the EU and Japan; US flat to declining; rapid growth in South/Southeast Asia and parts of the Middle East; Africa remains low but rising from a small base. Regional patterns track coal dependence and industrial structure (export manufacturing in Asia). Correlations: higher emissions align with higher carbon intensity, lower renewable share, greater fossil fuel use, and poorer urban air quality; efficiency gains and renewable expansion weaken these links. Outlook: declines in advanced economies and accelerating clean energy could bring a global peak this decade, but faster growth in emerging markets is the key uncertainty.

air_quality_pm2_5_exposure.summary: Air Quality (PM2.5 exposure) gauges the population‑weighted average concentration of fine particles ≤2.5µm (µg/m³), a major cardiopulmonary risk; lower is better. Top performers include Nordics and select oceanic/high‑latitude countries (e.g., Finland, Iceland, Sweden, New Zealand, Estonia) with strong standards and cleaner energy. Low performers cluster in South Asia (Bangladesh, India, Pakistan, Nepal) and parts of MENA where traffic, coal/biomass burning, and dust elevate levels. Trends: steady declines in China and much of Europe/US from tighter controls; episodic spikes from wildfires (North America, Australia) and crop‑residue burning (Indo‑Gangetic Plain). Urban centers exceed rural averages. Correlations: higher PM2.5 with fossil‑fuel intensity, coal reliance, traffic, open burning, and deforestation/fires; lower with renewables share, vehicle/industrial standards, and waste management. Outlook: gradual improvement, but climate‑driven wildfires, urban growth, and dust could stall gains in vulnerable regions.

internet_penetration_rate.summary:
Internet Penetration Rate (%): share of a country’s population with internet access. It underpins education, productivity, and social connectivity.
Top performers: Iceland, Norway, Denmark, Netherlands, Singapore, South Korea, UAE/Qatar typically exceed 90–95%. Low performers: Eritrea, South Sudan, Burundi, Somalia, CAR, Chad often below 20%.
Trends/regional patterns: Global access keeps rising, but mature markets are near saturation; fastest gains come from mobile broadband in South Asia and parts of Sub‑Saharan Africa. Europe/North America and advanced East Asia lead; Latin America is mid-to-high; MENA is split (GCC high, others mixed); Sub‑Saharan Africa lags with large rural gaps.
Correlations (Infrastructure & Technology): strongly linked to 4G/5G and fiber coverage, electricity reliability, device affordability, and digital literacy; also aligns with higher GDP per capita and e‑government uptake.
Outlook: Continued growth via cheaper devices, fiber/5G, and LEO satellites; closing affordability and skills gaps is critical.

employment_to_population_ratio.summary: Employment-to-population ratio (%) is the share of working‑age people who have jobs—showing how fully an economy uses its labor. Top performers typically include Iceland, Switzerland, the Netherlands and other Nordics; many Sub‑Saharan African economies also post high ratios (often driven by informal/necessity work). Low ratios are common in Middle East & North Africa (e.g., Jordan, Iraq) and parts of South Asia due to low female participation; South Africa is also low given high unemployment. Trends: broad post‑pandemic rebound in OECD, with lingering gaps where tourism/retail lag; aging economies sustain levels via higher 55–64 employment. Regional pattern: Nordics/East Asia high, Continental Europe mid, Southern Europe and MENA lower, Latin America mixed. Correlations: positive with labor‑force participation, negative with unemployment; shaped by informality, education, and productivity. Outlook: stable to modestly rising, contingent on growth, childcare and activation policies; risks from slowdown and aging.

military_spending_sipri.summary: Military Spending (SIPRI) measures annual outlays on armed forces (pay, equipment, operations) in USD billions. Top spenders: US (by far), China, Russia, India, Saudi Arabia, plus UK, Germany, France. Lowest in absolute terms are microstates and low-income economies in the Pacific, Caribbean, and Sub-Saharan Africa (often under $1 bn). Global totals at record highs; sharp rises in Europe since 2022, steady build-ups in Asia-Pacific, persistently high Middle East; Latin America/Africa flatter. Correlations: higher where conflict risk, great-power rivalry and alliance commitments (e.g., NATO) are stronger; aligns with arms imports, personnel, and defense burden (% GDP). Outlook: Further increases likely amid tensions and modernization (cyber, drones), tempered by debt/fiscal limits.

education_expenditure_of_gdp.summary: Education expenditure (% of GDP) tracks the share of national output invested in education—an indicator of human capital priorities. Top allocators (often >7%) include Cuba, Iceland/Nordics, and several Southern African countries (Namibia, Botswana, Lesotho). Low shares (<3%) appear in parts of South Asia (e.g., Bangladesh, Pakistan) and some high‑income resource exporters in the Gulf (e.g., Qatar, UAE), where large GDPs depress the ratio despite solid per‑student outlays. Regionally, Nordics and much of Latin America cluster around or above the global average (~4–6%); many lower‑income Asian countries lag; Sub‑Saharan Africa often shows high % but low absolute spend per student. Correlations: higher shares generally align with higher enrollment/completion, lower pupil‑teacher ratios, and improved learning outcomes, though efficiency and governance mediate results; GDP per capita drives absolute spending capacity. Trend: post‑pandemic recovery with SDG4 commitments. Outlook: gradual increases in LMICs, prioritizing targeted, efficient investments.

military_expenditure_of_gdp.summary:
Military Expenditure (% of GDP) tracks defense’s share of national output, signaling fiscal burden and security priorities.

Top shares cluster in active-conflict and Gulf states—e.g., Ukraine (surged since 2022), Israel, Saudi Arabia, Oman, and Russia. Lowest shares appear in countries without standing armies (Costa Rica, Iceland) and low-threat settings (Panama, Ireland, Japan). The U.S. sits above OECD norms; many EU members hover near the 2% NATO target but are trending upward.

Regional patterns: MENA and Eastern Europe are elevated; Latin America and much of Southeast Asia are low; Sub‑Saharan Africa is mixed with conflict-driven spikes.

Correlations (Security & Defense): typically positive with arms imports, active-duty personnel per capita, and battle-related deaths; high spending does not guarantee lower internal violence.

Outlook: Ongoing wars and great‑power rivalry keep ratios high in Eastern Europe and MENA; NATO commitments lift Europe; post‑conflict normalization and fiscal pressures may cap growth elsewhere.

olympic_medals_summer.summary: Olympic Medals (Summer) counts total podiums per country, reflecting elite performance, sports culture depth, and long-term investment. Top performers remain the United States, China, and Russia (incl. USSR/ROC), with Germany, Great Britain, Japan, Australia, France, and Italy consistently strong. Low totals are common among small island states and low-income nations, many in Sub‑Saharan Africa and microstates with limited facilities. Trends: rising East Asia (notably China, Japan), a UK surge since 2012 via targeted funding, host‑nation boosts, and continued dominance by wealthier, larger countries; Eastern Europe’s share has softened since the 1990s. Regional gaps persist: Europe/North America dense medal bases; Latin America led by Brazil/Cuba; Africa excels in distance running but has modest overall counts. Likely correlates within Sports & Culture: sports participation, facility access, school PE coverage, national funding, elite centers, and event‑hosting capacity. Outlook: continued concentration at the top, with gradual gains where sustained pipelines and youth programs expand.

living_planet_index.summary: Living Planet Index (1970=1) tracks average abundance change across >30,000 vertebrate populations; values below 1 indicate proportional declines since 1970. The global trend is downward, with the steepest losses in tropical regions and freshwater species; Europe and North America show partial stabilization from pollution control, reforestation, and reintroductions. Top performers typically combine extensive protected areas and strong enforcement with limited habitat conversion (e.g., Bhutan, Costa Rica, some small island states with large MPAs). Low performers are concentrated where deforestation, overfishing, and land-use change are rapid (Amazon and Congo Basin nations, parts of Southeast Asia). Correlations: higher LPI with forest cover gain, protected-area coverage, sustainable fisheries; lower LPI with deforestation, ecological footprint, water stress, and pollution. Outlook: recovery is feasible but depends on scaling 30x30 protection, habitat restoration, and climate mitigation.

inform_resilience_index.summary: Resilience Index (0–10) gauges a country’s capacity to withstand and recover from disasters across institutions, infrastructure, and basic services; lower scores mean stronger resilience. Consistently low (best) scores are seen in high-income systems such as the Nordics, Japan, Singapore, Germany, and New Zealand. High (weaker) scores cluster in fragile or hazard-exposed states including Afghanistan, Haiti, Yemen, South Sudan, and DRC. Regionally, OECD Europe and advanced Asia perform best; Sub-Saharan Africa and conflict-affected MENA lag; small island states vary with exposure offsetting capacity. The index typically improves as government effectiveness, rule of law, social protection coverage, health capacity, and access to water/energy rise, and worsens with poverty, inequality, and conflict. Outlook: steady gains in middle-income countries via service expansion and early-warning systems, but climate shocks and instability remain key downside risks.
